title: Climate Resilience Starts With Care
gist: Caren Grown and Kendall Trelegan argue that climate-adaptation plans and the UNEP's $310-365 billion annual funding-need estimate omit climate-resilient care services, whose breakdown during shocks turns climate events into health and economic crises. They estimate climate-resilient care in Bangladesh would cost 3-5% of GDP and could employ 3.6-7 million people, and pitch care as an investable, evidence-rich adaptation asset ahead of COP31.

insights.claim: The UN Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $310-365 billion per year for climate adaptation through 2035, putting the current funding gap at $280 billion.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Quantifies a large unmet financing need that MDBs, climate funds and blended-finance vehicles are being asked to fill.
insights.quote: developing countries will need $310–365 billion per year through 2035, putting the current funding gap at $280 billion
insights.locator: Financing for adaptation activities remains nowhere

insights.claim: Deploying adaptation money may be an even bigger challenge than raising it, because institutions struggle to find implementation-ready adaptation investments whose risks can be properly assessed and priced.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Pipeline scarcity, not just capital scarcity, constrains adaptation finance; assets with measurable risk profiles are at a premium.
insights.locator: Financing for adaptation activities remains nowhere

insights.claim: With last year among the hottest on record and COP31 in Turkey approaching in November, governments must move beyond commitments and focus on implementing adaptation.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: COP31 is a near-term catalyst for adaptation-finance announcements.

insights.claim: Estimates of adaptation funding needs and investment pipelines overlook climate-adapted care services that help families prepare for, cope with and recover from climate hazards, so leaving care out underestimates what resilience actually requires.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Implies headline adaptation-need figures, including the $310-365 billion estimate, are too low.
insights.quote: Leaving care out of national adaptation plans thus means underestimating what climate resilience actually requires.
insights.locator: Leaving care out of national adaptation

insights.claim: Provisional estimates suggest at least 35,000 excess deaths occurred across Europe during this summer's back-to-back heat waves, with the absence of climate-adapted infrastructure and coordinated services contributing despite well-developed welfare systems.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Even rich economies face significant mortality costs from heat, signaling demand for heat-adapted health and care infrastructure in developed markets too.
insights.quote: at least 35,000 excess deaths occurred across Europe during this summer’s severe back-to-back heat waves

insights.claim: When floods and wildfires separate caregivers from dependents, a lack of formal care leads to preventable hospital admissions that add pressure to strained health services.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Care failures during climate shocks transmit into higher public health spending.

insights.so_what: Climate shocks can reduce labor-force participation, particularly among women, amplifying economic damage.

insights.claim: There is no standard definition of adaptation, and national estimates are built project by project mostly in conventional sectors, which lets care fall through the cracks.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Methodological gaps in adaptation accounting skew capital toward traditional infrastructure sectors.

insights.claim: Agriculture, forestry, fishing, water supply and sanitation account for nearly 40% of global adaptation finance, health receives an estimated 4-6% and education around 2%, while long-term care and early-childhood care and education are essentially absent, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Shows where adaptation capital currently flows and highlights social infrastructure as an underfunded segment.
insights.quote: Agriculture, forestry, fishing, water supply, and sanitation account for nearly 40% of global adaptation finance, while health receives an estimated 4–6% and education around 2%.

insights.claim: The already-too-low $310-365 billion figure is baked into national plans and multilateral-development-bank targets, yet intensifying climate shocks will increase care needs, with unpaid caregivers, overwhelmingly women and girls, filling the gap when formal services fall short.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Suggests MDB adaptation targets may need upward revision to include social infrastructure.

insights.claim: The authors estimate building climate-resilient care infrastructure in Bangladesh would require investment equal to roughly 3-5% of GDP, similar to what is needed for health and education, but only a fraction of the estimated value of unpaid care work.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Provides a sizing benchmark for care-infrastructure investment in a climate-vulnerable emerging market.
insights.quote: building climate-resilient care infrastructure in Bangladesh would require an investment equivalent to roughly 3–5% of GDP

insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Positions care investment as a large-scale job creator, with spillovers to construction and supply chains.

themes.theme: Care as an investable adaptation asset

insights.claim: Care services offer financiers a concrete way to deploy adaptation money because they come with an established evidence base on unit costs, staffing models, utilization and outcomes, which eases risk assessment.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Addresses the pipeline/risk-pricing bottleneck in adaptation finance, potentially making care a bankable adaptation category.

insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: Aging demographics provide structural demand for care infrastructure, supporting long-duration investment cases.

insights.claim: As adaptation financing tightens, every dollar must work harder, which strengthens the case for care systems that both build resilience and ease pressure on public budgets.
insights.speaker: CAREN GROWN
insights.so_what: In a constrained funding environment, projects with fiscal co-benefits are likely to be prioritized.
